title: The Seventeen Camels
text:
An old man died and left seventeen camels to his three sons. His will said that the eldest should have half of the camels, the second son a third, and the youngest a ninth.

The brothers set to work and quickly ran into trouble. Half of seventeen is eight and a half. A third is five and two thirds. A ninth is not quite two. No one wanted to cut up a camel, and each brother suspected the others of trying to get more than his share. The argument grew bitter, and the family seemed about to fall apart.

At last they went to a wise man and asked for help. He listened, thought for a while, and then said he would lend them one of his own camels. Now there were eighteen.

Half of eighteen is nine, so the eldest took nine camels. A third of eighteen is six, so the second son took six. A ninth of eighteen is two, so the youngest took two. Nine and six and two make seventeen. One camel was left over: the wise man's own. He took it back and went home, and the brothers were satisfied.
lesson: When a negotiation is stuck, look for something you can add to the table, even temporarily, that lets everyone see a solution that was there all along.
caveat: The tale's origin is uncertain; it works because the father's fractions add up to only seventeen eighteenths of the herd.
